label: Levi-Civita Connection
notes: Open the chapter as a repair to a tempting but wrong operation. Differentiating a tangent vector field in ambient space usually leaves the tangent plane, so the lecture asks what part of that derivative belongs intrinsically to the surface.

label: What The Connection Must Do
notes: Use this slide as the contract for the hour. The connection has to split ambient differentiation, agree with metric data, feed the shape operator identities, and finally explain why Gaussian curvature is preserved by isometry.

label: The Surface Laboratory
notes: The graph patch keeps the computations honest. Its tangent vectors and second derivatives are explicit, the metric is not constant, and the normal component is visible. That makes it a good place to see where Christoffel symbols come from.

label: Tangential Differentiation
notes: Stress that the ambient derivative is not discarded or magically tangent. It is decomposed into a tangent projection and a normal remainder. The tangent projection is the Levi-Civita derivative, while the normal coefficient is the second fundamental form.

label: Christoffel Symbols
notes: This is the main computational bridge. One route projects second derivatives of the surface into the tangent basis. The other route differentiates the metric. Their agreement is the concrete sign that the same connection has both extrinsic and intrinsic descriptions.

label: Metric Compatibility And No Torsion
notes: Present the characterization as a uniqueness test rather than a memory exercise. Metric compatibility says inner products differentiate by the product rule, and torsion-free says coordinate directions commute through the connection. Together these two constraints are enough to solve for the Christoffel symbols from the metric, so there is no hidden embedding data in the derivative.

label: Covariant Derivative Of A Field
notes: Now move from basis vectors to arbitrary tangent fields. The derivative of the coefficient functions is the visible change in coordinates, and the Gamma term corrects for the fact that the coordinate basis itself turns across the surface.

label: The Shape Operator Enters
notes: The connection also differentiates endomorphisms such as the shape operator. Codazzi says that the covariant derivative of A has the symmetry forced by being the second derivative data of an actual embedded surface. In computations, it is a consistency test: the first and second fundamental forms must belong to the same parametrized surface.

label: Gauss Equation
notes: Connection curvature measures the noncommutativity of covariant differentiation. On a surface, that operator is completely controlled by Gaussian curvature and the metric area rotation. This is the hinge between extrinsic shape and intrinsic curvature, because the determinant of the shape operator can be recovered from connection curvature.

label: Theorema Egregium
notes: Keep the dependency chain explicit. If the metric determines the connection and the connection curvature determines K through the Gauss equation, then any isometry carries the same K. The surprise is not that K can be computed from shape, but that it does not need shape.

label: Metric-Only Model Checks
notes: These examples keep the theorem from feeling abstract. The plane and cylinder share flat intrinsic metric data even though one sits curved in space. The sphere metric has nonzero connection coefficients and produces K equal to one.

label: Residual Diagnostics
notes: Read the numerical notebook artifacts as a debugging dashboard. Small interior residuals mean the projection, metric, Gauss, and Codazzi computations agree. Boundary artifacts are expected from finite differences, but interior growth points to a sign or indexing mistake.

label: Common Sign And Index Traps
notes: This slide is a preemptive repair station. Most failed computations in this chapter come from changing the normal orientation, using the wrong area rotation sign, forgetting the Gamma correction, or mixing metric and shape data from different surfaces.

label: Chapter Takeaways
notes: Close by compressing the lecture into four transformations. Ambient derivatives become tangent derivatives, projection coefficients become metric formulas, shape data must satisfy compatibility equations, and Gaussian curvature becomes an intrinsic quantity. That is the chapter's bridge from concrete surface calculations to Riemannian geometry.
